questions.question: How do you get the length of a string?
questions.answer:
The length property returns the number of UTF-16 code units in the string, which matches the visible character count for most text.

code:
console.log('playwright'.length);  // 10

real example:
Truncating long failure messages in test reporters by checking .length before slicing keeps logs readable without hard crashes.

questions.question: What is the difference between indexOf and includes on a string?
questions.answer:
includes returns a boolean for whether the substring exists, while indexOf returns the first position or -1 when not found.

code:
console.log('video/invoice'.includes('invoice'));  // true
console.log('video/invoice'.indexOf('invoice'));   // 6

real example:
Asserting that a redirect URL contains the expected route with expect(url).toContain('/checkout') is a common Playwright pattern.

questions.question: What does slice do and how does it differ from substring?
questions.answer:
slice returns a portion of the string by start and end index. Both treat negative arguments as counting from the end, but substring clamps negatives to 0, making slice more predictable.

code:
console.log('trader'.slice(1, 4));   // ra
console.log('trader'.slice(-2));     // er

real example:
Extracting a slug from a URL segment with slice keeps the parsing deterministic even when the segment length varies.

questions.question: Why should you always call trim() on text scraped from a page?
questions.answer:
trim removes leading and trailing whitespace, and scraped text often contains newlines or padding. Comparing untrimmed text causes assertions to fail on invisible characters.

code:
const text = '  Login  ';
console.log(text.trim());  // 'Login'

real example:
Playwright assertions like await expect(page.getByText('Login')).toBeVisible() can fail because textContent includes formatting whitespace that trim() removes.

questions.question: How do you convert a string to uppercase or lowercase?
questions.answer:
Use toUpperCase() or toLowerCase(), both of which return new strings because strings are immutable.

code:
console.log('login'.toUpperCase());  // 'LOGIN'
console.log('LOGIN'.toLowerCase());  // 'login'

real example:
Case-insensitive assertions normalize both sides with toLowerCase() before comparing user-facing text like country names or error messages.

questions.question: What does split do and what does join do?
questions.answer:
split divides a string into an array by a separator, and join merges an array back into a string with a separator.

code:
const parts = 'a,b,c'.split(',');
console.log(parts);                 // ['a','b','c']
console.log(parts.join('-'));       // 'a-b-c'

real example:
Parsing a comma-separated tags header or building CSV test fixtures are both natural split and join workflows.

questions.question: What is the difference between replace and replaceAll?
questions.answer:
replace substitutes only the first match, while replaceAll substitutes every match. Passing a regex with the global flag also replaces all matches.

code:
console.log('a-b-a'.replace('-', '_'));      // 'a_b-a'
console.log('a-b-a'.replaceAll('-', '_'));   // 'a_b_a'

real example:
Sanitizing an API ID that may contain multiple dashes with replaceAll prevents partial replacements from breaking downstream selectors.

questions.question: How do template literals interpolate values?
questions.answer:
Template literals use backticks and embed values with ${expression}, where any JavaScript expression is evaluated and converted to a string.

code:
const name = 'Ana';
console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);  // Hello, Ana!

real example:
Building dynamic locators like page.getByText(`Order #${orderId}`) reads far better than string concatenation with plus signs.

questions.question: How do you check if a string starts or ends with a given substring?
questions.answer:
Use startsWith and endsWith, which return booleans and are case-sensitive by default.

code:
const url = 'https://api.test.com/v1';
console.log(url.startsWith('https://'));  // true
console.log(url.endsWith('/v1'));         // true

real example:
Validating API base URLs and env-specific endpoints before tests hit them avoids sending requests to the wrong host.

questions.question: What does padStart do?
questions.answer:
padStart fills the beginning of a string with a filler until it reaches a target length, which is useful for padding ids and timestamps.

code:
console.log('42'.padStart(5, '0'));  // '00042'

real example:
Generating deterministic test order numbers with fixed digit counts keeps parallel test data readable in dashboards.

questions.question: Are strings mutable or immutable in JavaScript?
questions.answer:
Strings are immutable. Every string method that changes content returns a brand-new string, and the original value stays untouched.

code:
const s = 'hello';
const u = s.toUpperCase();
console.log(s);  // 'hello'
console.log(u);  // 'HELLO'

real example:
When storing original page text and a transformed copy, immutability guarantees the asserted original is never corrupted by transforms.

questions.question: What is the difference between charAt and bracket indexing?
questions.answer:
charAt('hello'.charAt(0)) returns the character or an empty string when out of range, while bracket indexing returns undefined for missing positions.

code:
console.log('hello'.charAt(9));  // ''
console.log('hello'[9]);         // undefined

real example:
Bracket indexing that returns undefined is a common source of hidden bugs when assertion messages interpolate a missing character.

questions.question: How do you write multi-line strings without escape sequences?
questions.answer:
Template literals with backticks preserve real newlines, so you can write multi-line text directly without escaping newline characters.

code:
const message = `Line one
Line two`;
console.log(message);

real example:
Multi-line request bodies and SQL fixtures in tests stay readable, which helps code review catch wrong assertions faster.

questions.question: What is the difference between innerText and textContent reminders for scraped text?
How do you convert a string to an array of characters?
questions.answer:
Use split('') with an empty separator, or the Array.from() function which also handles unicode correctly.

code:
console.log('abc'.split(''));    // ['a','b','c']
console.log(Array.from('abc')); // ['a','b','c']

real example:
Reversing a code and checking it against an expected layout uses character arrays that make each digit individually assertable.
